ResourceHeader.ResourceName: Active Magnetosphere and Planetary Electrodynamics Response Experiment

RevisionEvent.Note: Initial SPASE 2.7.1 XML resource description submission, metadata submitted by Rebecca Ringuette

ResourceHeader.Description: The Active Magnetosphere and Planetary Electrodynamics Response Experiment (AMPERE) is a facility of the National Science Foundation Geospace Cluster (AGS-GC) implemented by The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. The Iridium Communications system consists of 66 satellites plus on-orbit spares in 780km altitude, circular, near-polar orbits in six equally spaced orbit planes with eleven satellites in each plane. Each satellite carries an engineering magnetometer with approximately 30 nT resolution. Techniques have been developed at JHU/APL to process Iridium magnetic field data and obtain global maps of magnetic perturbations due to field aligned currents linking the ionosphere and magnetosphere. AMPERE provides a re-sampling cadence of around 9 minutes and continuous 24/7 coverage throughout all levels of geomagnetic activity. Derived data products include global maps of the Birkeland currents and key parameters including Birkeland current indices, auroral oval size, and the total Birkeland current. AMPERE spans both generations of Iridium satellites, Block 1 from October 2009 through 2018, and NEXT from 2019 forward, with a transition from January 2017 to May 2019. The noise level in Block 1 processed data is 70 to 100 nT while it is better in NEXT, about 40 nT. AMPERE products have been used extensively resulting in over 200 publications on topics including substorms, storms, polar cap dynamics, convection dynamics, ring current development, and simulation/modeling comparisons. Data and derived products are all available from https://ampere.jhuapl.edu. AMPERE is made possible by NSF sponsorship under the following grants: 739864 (2008-2013); 1420184 (2014-2020); 2002574 (2020-2026); 2537345 (2026-2028).
